claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a homogeneous single-phase solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength but favorable plasticity and machinability.
The mechanical-property combination is governed by the absence of nanoscale precipitates that impede dislocation motion.
A controlled aging heat treatment can form nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains in CoCrFeNiTi without changing its overall composition.
The induced nanoscale precipitates pin or otherwise obstruct dislocations.
Precipitate-induced obstruction of dislocations increases hardness.
Precipitate-induced obstruction of dislocations increases compressive or tensile strength.
Precipitate-induced obstruction of dislocations reduces plasticity.
Precipitate-induced obstruction of dislocations reduces machinability.
Relative to the as-cast single-phase alloy, the aged alloy will have higher hardness.
Relative to the as-cast single-phase alloy, the aged alloy will have higher compressive or tensile strength.
Relative to the as-cast single-phase alloy, the aged alloy will exhibit a measurable decrease in plastic strain.
The magnitudes of strengthening, hardening, and plasticity loss depend on precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
The hypothesis is intended to apply from 25 °C to 600 °C under quasi-static uniaxial loading at strain rates around 10^-3 s^-1.
Failure to observe increased hardness and strength or decreased plasticity after confirmed nanoscale precipitation would falsify the hypothesis.
